Jihlava
YIH-lah-vah
n. (the Moravian mining town, German Iglau, where the Compacts of Basel were solemnly proclaimed to the kingdom of Bohemia in 1436)
Czech Jihlava, from the river of that name, perhaps from jehla, a needle, for its sharp stones; German Iglau.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Jihlava is the town where the one formal agreement between Rome and a reforming body before Trent was read out and sworn. A German-speaking silver-mining town on the Bohemian-Moravian border, it was chosen as neutral ground, and on 5 July 1436 the Compacts negotiated at the Council of Basel were proclaimed there to the estates of Bohemia and Moravia: the laity of the kingdom might receive the cup, and the kingdom was received back into communion with the church. Sigismund was acknowledged king in the same place. The Compacts were the Hussites' victory and their defeat at once. They granted the cup and conceded nothing on the free preaching of the word, the holding of civil property by clergy, or the punishing of public sin, which were the other three of the Four Articles; and Rome never ratified what its legates at Basel had signed, Pius II declaring them void in 1462. Jihlava itself turned Lutheran in the sixteenth century and was recatholicised after 1620. The dictionary enters Jihlava because the Compacts are the first worked example of a reform settling for the concession it could get, and of what such a settlement is worth when the other party does not regard itself as bound.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a compact as an agreement between parties; to ratify as to confirm or establish; a concession as the act of yielding or granting; and union as the act of joining two or more things into one.

expand to see more

COMPACT, n. An agreement; a contract between parties; a covenant or mutual engagement.

RATIFY, v. To confirm; to establish; to settle; to approve and sanction what has been done by an agent.

CONCESSION, n. The act of granting or yielding; usually implying a demand, claim or request from the party to whom it is made.

UNION, n. The act of joining two or more things into one, and thus forming a compound body or a mixture.

AGREE, v. To be of one mind; to harmonize in opinion; to live in concord.

Key Scripture

Amo 3:3 — "Can two walk together, except they be agreed?"

Isa 8:20 — "To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them."

1Co 1:10 — "Now I beseech you, brethren, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that ye all speak the same thing, and that there be no divisions among you; but that ye be perfectly joined together in the same mind and in the same judgment."

Heb 10:36 — "For ye have need of patience, that, after ye have done the will of God, ye might receive the promise."

Modern Corruption

Moravian mining town where the Compacts of Basel were proclaimed in 1436, granting the cup to the Bohemian laity and conceding nothing else.

expand to see more

The corruption to be named is the agreement that buys peace by leaving the doctrine unsettled. The Compacts gave the Bohemians the cup and left the mass, the priesthood, purgatory and the invocation of saints exactly as they were, and both parties signed knowing that the question of authority underneath had not been touched. “Can two walk together, except they be agreed?” (Amo 3:3) is the question the Compacts did not ask, and Pius II answered it in 1462 by declaring them void, which is what an unsettled agreement is always worth to the stronger party.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that unity is a unity in the truth confessed, not a formula that lets two doctrines stand. “that ye all speak the same thing” (1Co 1:10) is the standard, and it is met by agreement on what is believed and not by a licence to differ. Jihlava also teaches patience in the right place: the Brethren, who refused the Compacts as insufficient and had no settlement at all, were still a church in 1620 when the Utraquist establishment built on the Compacts had almost nothing left to lose, and of them it may be said that they had “need of patience” (Heb 10:36) and kept it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek sumphoneo (G4856), to agree together; Hebrew torah (H8451), law, instruction; Greek schisma (G4978), a rent, a division.

expand to see more

Hebrew yaad (H3259) — to appoint, to meet by agreement; “Can two walk together, except they be agreed?”, Amos 3:3.

Hebrew torah (H8451) — law, instruction, that which is taught; “To the law and to the testimony”, Isaiah 8:20.

Greek schisma (G4978) — a rent, a cleft, a division in a body; “that there be no divisions among you”, 1 Corinthians 1:10.

Greek katartizo (G2675) — to mend, to fit together, to make complete; “that ye be perfectly joined together”, 1 Corinthians 1:10.

Greek hupomone (G5281) — patience, endurance under trial; “ye have need of patience”, Hebrews 10:36.

Usage

"“Can two walk together, except they be agreed?” (Amo 3:3) — the Compacts proclaimed on 5 July 1436."

"“that ye all speak the same thing” (1Co 1:10) — one ceremony granted and four doctrines left standing."

"“ye have need of patience” (Heb 10:36) — the Brethren who refused the settlement and outlasted it."
